### 1. Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [cognitive-science, formative-assessment, k-12, learning-engineering, math-strategies]
```

Published September 2007. Panel: Harold Pashler (chair, UC San Diego), Patrice M. Bain, Brian A. Bottge, Arthur Graesser, Kenneth Koedinger (CMU), Mark McDaniel, Janet Metcalfe. Seven recommendations for using learning and study time effectively in subjects requiring content mastery (science, social studies, mathematics): spacing content review, alternating worked examples with practice problems, combining visual and verbal instruction, linking abstract and concrete concepts, strategic use of quizzes, efficient study time allocation, and deep explanatory questioning.

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/12"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"

description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [data-sharing, formative-assessment, k-12, learning-engineering, professional-development]
```

Published September 2009. Panel: Laura Hamilton (chair, RAND Corporation), Richard Halverson, Sharnell S. Jackson, Ellen Mandinach, Jonathan A. Supovitz, Jeffrey C. Wayman. Five recommendations for leveraging student data to monitor academic progress and evaluate teaching: establishing schoolwide data systems, fostering a data-informed culture, integrating data review into instructional improvement cycles, teaching students to interpret their own performance data for goal-setting, and implementing district-level evidence infrastructure.

```yaml
doi: null

tags: [k-12, learning-engineering, math-education, math-strategies, math-word-problems]
```

Published May 2012, revised October 2018. Panel: John Woodward (chair), Sybilla Beckmann, Mark Driscoll, Megan Franke, Patricia Herzig, Asha Jitendra, Kenneth R. Koedinger (CMU), Philip Ogbuehi. Prepared by Mathematica. Five recommendations for teachers, math coaches, and curriculum developers targeting grades 4–8: preparing problems for whole-class instruction, supporting student self-monitoring and reflection, teaching visual representation, exposing students to multiple solution strategies, and helping students recognize mathematical concepts and notation.

### 4. Teaching Math to Young Children

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/18"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [early-childhood, k-12, learning-engineering, math-education, prekindergarten]
```

Published November 2013. Panel: Douglas Frye (chair), Arthur J. Baroody, Margaret Burchinal, Sharon M. Carver, Nancy C. Jordan, Judy McDowell. Five recommendations for preschool, prekindergarten, and kindergarten educators: teaching number and operations using developmental progression (Moderate Evidence), teaching geometry and patterns developmentally (Minimal Evidence), using progress monitoring aligned to individual child knowledge (Minimal Evidence), teaching mathematical perspectives on everyday situations (Minimal Evidence), and dedicating daily math time integrated throughout instruction (Minimal Evidence). Each recommendation includes implementation steps and solutions for common obstacles.

### 10. CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines 3.0

```yaml
url: "https://udlguidelines.cast.org"
type: framework
source: "CAST"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [cognitive-science, inclusive-design, k-12, learning-engineering]
```

Released July 30, 2024. Organization: CAST. An educational framework "based on scientific insights into how humans learn" designed as "a tool that can be applied in any discipline or domain to ensure that all learners are able to access and participate in meaningful, challenging learning opportunities." Version 3.0 specifically addresses "critical barriers rooted in biases and systems of exclusion for learners with and without disabilities." Three design principles: Engagement, Representation, and Action & Expression. Overarching goal: learner agency that is "purposeful & reflective, resourceful & authentic, strategic & action-oriented." Downloadable PDF available in 20+ languages. Audience: educators, curriculum developers, learning and instructional designers, researchers, parents.

Establishes that "the protection of human rights and dignity is the cornerstone" of the framework. ### 16. Lenses on Literature — Evidence for ESSA

```yaml
url: "https://evidenceforessa.org/program/lenses-on-literature/"
type: report
source: "Evidence for ESSA"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [carnegie-learning, computer-assisted-learning, formative-assessment, k-12, learning-engineering]
```

Evidence review published at Evidence for ESSA (Johns Hopkins University). Carnegie Learning's Lenses on Literature (formerly Literacy Design Collaborative) earned a "Promising" (Tier 3) ESSA evidence rating. Instructional framework emphasizing daily, standards-driven reading, writing, and discourse organized around disciplinary literacy with complex texts. Primary study: 18,203 students across Kentucky and Pennsylvania (2012–2013). Effect size: +0.05 average; Kentucky: +0.06 (statistically significant); Pennsylvania: +0.03 (non-significant). Includes scaffolds for multilingual learners, embedded assessments using Stanford-aligned rubrics, and professional development with coaching and data analysis.

### 17. The State of Educational Data Mining in 2009: A Review and Future Visions

```yaml
url: "https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/8"
type: paper
source: "Journal of Educational Data Mining"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: "10.5281/zenodo.3554657"
license: "CC BY-NC-ND 4.0"
tags: [computer-assisted-learning, intelligent-tutoring, jedm, learning-engineering, meta-analysis]
```

Published 2009. Authors: Ryan S.J.d. Baker (Worcester Polytechnic Institute), Kalina Yacef (University of Sydney). Journal of Educational Data Mining, Vol. 1, No. 1. Inaugural-issue review paper for the EDM field: examines the history and methodological evolution of educational data mining, comparing early approaches with 2008–2009 research. Identifies three field-wide trends: increased emphasis on prediction methods, emergence of discovery-with-models techniques, and declining focus on relationship mining. Catalogues the most-cited EDM papers published 1995–2005 and analyzes their influence within and beyond the field. Open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

### 20. Shifting Mindsets: Designing Lessons for Learner Variability

```yaml

type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary

license: null

```

Digital Promise pilot study conducted with DonorsChoose examining whether teachers could use the Learner Variability Navigator (LVN)—a free, open-source web app curating whole-child research and evidence-based strategies—to customize instruction for diverse learners. ### 21. Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Response to Intervention (RtI) for Elementary and Middle Schools

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/2"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, learning-engineering, math-education, math-strategies, response-to-intervention, wwc]
```

Published April 2009. Panel: Russell Gersten (chair, Instructional Research Group), Sybilla Beckmann, Benjamin Clarke, Anne Foegen, Laurel Marsh, Jon R. Star, Bradley Witzel. Eight recommendations for elementary and middle school math intervention using the Response to Intervention framework: screen all students and provide targeted support (Moderate), emphasize whole numbers K–5 and rational numbers grades 4–8 (Minimal), use explicit and systematic instruction (Strong), teach problem solving via common structural patterns (Strong), incorporate visual representations (Moderate), build fact fluency with approximately 10 minutes per session (Moderate), monitor student progress throughout intervention (Minimal), and include motivational strategies in secondary and tertiary intervention tiers (Minimal).

### 22. Assisting Students Struggling with Reading: Response to Intervention (RtI) and Multi-Tier Intervention in the Primary Grades

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/3"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, learning-engineering, literacy, response-to-intervention, wwc]
```

Published February 2009. Panel: Russell Gersten (chair), Donald Compton, Carol M. Connor, Joseph Dimino, Lana Santoro, Sylvia Linan-Thompson, W. David Tilly. Five recommendations for primary-grade reading intervention using a multi-tier approach: screen all students for reading problems at the beginning and middle of the year (Moderate), provide differentiated reading instruction based on current assessments (Minimal), deliver intensive systematic instruction on up to three foundational reading skills in small groups for below-benchmark students (Strong), monitor tier 2 student progress monthly (Minimal), and deliver daily intensive instruction to tier 3 students showing minimal progress (Minimal).

### 25. Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/6"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null

```

Published December 2007. Panel: Russell Gersten (chair), Scott K. Baker, Penny Collins, Sylvia Linan-Thompson, Robin Scarcella, Timothy Shanahan. Five recommendations for literacy instruction with elementary English learners: screen for reading problems and monitor progress in English (Strong), provide intensive small-group reading interventions for at-risk students (Strong), deliver extensive and varied vocabulary instruction throughout the school day (Strong), make formal academic English development a key instructional goal beginning in primary grades (Minimal), and schedule regular peer-assisted learning for structured academic collaboration approximately 90 minutes weekly (Strong).

### 26. Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/7"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, learning-engineering, wwc]
```

Published May 2008. Panel: Rebecca Herman (chair, American Institutes for Research), Priscilla Dawson, Thomas Dee, Jay Greene, Rebecca Maynard, Sam Redding, Marlene Darwin. Four recommendations for school turnaround leaders: signal the need for dramatic change with leadership communicating urgency to staff and stakeholders; maintain a consistent focus on improving instruction by leveraging data to set goals and reassess learning continuously; make visible improvements early in the turnaround process to motivate staff and reduce resistance; and build a committed staff aligned with improvement objectives.

### 30. Improving Reading Comprehension in Kindergarten Through 3rd Grade

Published September 2010. Panel: Timothy Shanahan (chair, University of Chicago), Kim Callison, Christine Carriere, Nell K. Duke (Michigan State), P. David Pearson (UC-Berkeley), Christopher Schatschneider (Florida State/FCRR), Joseph Torgesen (Florida State/FCRR). Five recommendations for K–3 reading comprehension: train students to apply reading comprehension strategies (Strong), instruct students to leverage text structure for comprehension and retention (Moderate), facilitate substantive dialogue about textual meaning (Minimal), choose materials strategically to foster comprehension growth (Minimal), and establish an engaging and motivating context for reading instruction (Moderate).

### 31. Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/15"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, learning-engineering, math-education, math-strategies, wwc]
```

Published September 2010. Panel: Robert Siegler (chair, Carnegie Mellon University), Thomas Carpenter, Francis Fennell, David Geary (University of Missouri), James Lewis, Yukari Okamoto, Laurie Thompson, Jonathan Wray. Five recommendations for fractions instruction grades K–8: build on students' informal understanding of sharing and proportionality; establish that fractions are numbers that expand the number system beyond whole numbers; support understanding of the reasoning behind fraction computation procedures; develop conceptual understanding of ratio, rate, and proportion before introducing cross-multiplication; and improve teachers' own fraction knowledge through professional development. Emphasizes number lines as a central teaching tool across grade levels.

Four recommendations for grades 1–6 writing instruction: provide daily time for students to write (Minimal), teach students to use the writing process for a variety of purposes (Strong), teach fluency with handwriting, spelling, sentence construction, typing, and word processing (Moderate), and create an engaged community of writers (Minimal).


Published November 2016. Panel: Thomas Bailey (chair, Teachers College, Columbia), Joanne Bashford, Angela Boatman (Vanderbilt), John Squires (Southern Regional Education Board), Michael Weiss (MDRC). Six recommendations for college administrators, advisors, and faculty serving academically underprepared postsecondary students: use multiple measures to assess readiness and place students (Minimal), enhance advising through required or incentivized regular participation (Moderate), implement monetary performance incentives (Moderate), redesign developmental education through compression or mainstreaming (Minimal), teach self-regulated learning strategies (Minimal), and create comprehensive integrated support programs (Moderate).

### 36. Preventing Dropout in Secondary Schools

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/24"
type: framework
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [dropout-prevention, k-12, learning-engineering, personalized-learning, wwc]
```

Published September 2017. Panel: Russell W. Rumberger (chair, UC Santa Barbara), Howard Addis, Elaine Allensworth (University of Chicago Consortium), Robert Balfanz (Johns Hopkins), Debra Duardo, Mark Dynarski. Updated version of the 2008 dropout prevention guide, incorporating nine additional years of research. Four recommendations for grades 6–12: monitor all students and proactively intervene on early signs of attendance, behavior, or academic problems (Minimal); deliver tailored support to students who have fallen behind and face substantial barriers (Moderate); involve students through educational offerings bridging learning to college and career while building resilience (Strong); and for schools with many at-risk students, establish small personalized learning communities for better tracking and assistance (Moderate).

Five recommendations for community college administrators, faculty, and staff: structure pathways enabling students to advance education, secure employment, and progress professionally (Moderate); provide contextualized basic skills training accelerating pathway entry and completion (Moderate); offer flexible schedules and instructional models boosting credential completion (Minimal); coordinate comprehensive student services to enhance credit accumulation (Moderate); and develop strategic employer and community partnerships preparing students for labor market success (Moderate).

### 201. Evidence for ESSA: Reading Partners

### 202. Evidence for ESSA: Success for All

Success for All is a comprehensive K–5 school reform program combining phonics instruction, cooperative learning, small-group tutoring, and frequent regrouping for high-poverty schools. ### 203. Evidence for ESSA: Reading Recovery

```yaml

description_inferred: false
```

Reading Recovery targets first-graders in the lowest 20–30% of their cohort, delivering daily 30-minute one-to-one lessons from specially trained teachers covering fluency, decoding, phonemic awareness, and guided reading. ### 204. Evidence for ESSA: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS) — Reading

### 230. Principled Transformers for Predictive Performance in Knowledge Tracing

```yaml
url: "https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/961"
```

### 232. Deep Learning vs. Bayesian Knowledge Tracing: Student Models for Interventions

### 233. The Continuous Hint Factory - Providing Hints in Vast and Sparsely Populated Edit Distance Spaces

### 237. When is Deep Learning the Best Approach to Knowledge Tracing?

Empirically compares logistic regression, deep learning, and Markov-based approaches to knowledge tracing across nine real-world datasets. ### 276. Advancing Multimodal Collaboration Analytics: A Scoping Review

```yaml
url: "https://learning-analytics.info/index.php/JLA/article/view/8625"
type: paper
source: "Journal of Learning Analytics"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-learning-platforms, jla, learning-engineering, meta-analysis, qualitative-research]
```

Reviews 36 empirical studies in multimodal collaboration analytics (MMCA), developing a definitional framework comprising five modality categories: auditory, visual, physiological, kinesthetic, and tactile. The study reveals that modality combinations in MMCA arise from technical, practical/pedagogical, methodological, or theoretical rationales, each contributing differently to insights about collaborative learning. The authors conclude that MMCA pursues comprehensive understanding of learner interactions during collaboration, moving beyond the constraints of analyzing individual data streams in isolation.

### 277. Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model

```yaml
url: "https://learning-analytics.info/index.php/JLA/article/view/7639"
type: paper
source: "Journal of Learning Analytics"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [computer-assisted-learning, digital-learning-platforms, formative-assessment, intelligent-tutoring, jla, k-12, math-education]
```

Creates a mathematics educational game called The Nomads targeting rational number arithmetic and applies a continuous conjunctive model (CCM) for cognitive diagnostic assessment of player data. Unlike traditional diagnostic models, CCM generates parameters at the attribute level and offers more parsimonious diagnoses using continuous variables, lending itself well to the dynamic nature of game-based learning. Learners' attribute mastery improved during gameplay and learners benefited from scaffolding on three of the game's instructed attributes.

### 280. Interpreting Predictive Learning Sequences in a College Math Course through a Self-Regulated Learning Framework

Collects multimodal data from 49 undergraduates completing a college math task — including digital interaction logs, think-aloud protocols, and self-reports — to validate which digital event sequences predict post-test performance. Scoping review of 14 peer-reviewed empirical studies (2011–2023) on multimodal learning analytics in elementary K–8 education, finding varied applications but consistent gaps: studies rarely describe data fusion techniques or address ethics and transparency requirements. This 2006 Campbell systematic review examined five experimental studies of after-school programs combining academics with youth development and recreation activities. This 2019 Campbell systematic review analyzed 43 studies (1992–2017) of linguistic comprehension interventions in preschool and school-aged children. Only 11% of first-time students placed into credit-bearing ELA courses under the new system compared to 22% previously; students in intensive pathways of credit-bearing courses showed the highest passing rates. The writing component did not predict any outcomes, leading the authors to recommend CMI consider removing it and weighting high school GPA more heavily.

### 344. Evidence and Gap Map of Tier 2 Literacy Interventions for Grades K–3 in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands

### 350. Exploring Implementation of Trauma-Engaged Practices in Alaska Schools

### 352. Principal Retention Patterns in Arizona, Nevada, and Utah

```yaml

date_added: 2026-05-01
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, longitudinal, professional-development]
```

REL West (REL 2021-129) examined principal retention across Arizona, Nevada, and Utah, finding that fewer than half of principals in each state remained at the same school over the four-year period from fall 2016 to fall 2020. Retention rates varied significantly by school performance level, with substantially lower retention at lower-performing schools. When principals left their positions, those who remained in the profession tended to transfer within the same school district rather than to a different district.

### 355. An Examination of the Costs of Texas Community Colleges

The AI-enabled edtech adoption cycle presents four interconnected phases—Vision and Planning, Implementation, Ongoing Evaluation, and Vision and Planning—emphasizing that AI-enabled EdTech adoption is not a linear process but an ongoing cycle of improvement. By integrating these considerations, institutions can more effectively leverage AI technologies to enhance teaching and learning outcomes while ensuring sustainable, equitable implementation.

### 395. Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC)

```yaml
url: "https://civilrightsdata.ed.gov/about"
type: dataset
source: "U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-02
doi: null
license: null
tags: [data-sharing, english-learners, k-12, open-datasets, school-discipline]
```

The Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) has collected civil rights data related to students' access and barriers to educational opportunity from early childhood through grade 12 since 1968, and since the 2011–12 collection has been administered every two years to all public school districts and schools in the 50 states and Washington, D.C. The CRDC collects information on student enrollment, access to courses, programs, and school staff, and school climate factors such as bullying, harassment, and student discipline, with most data disaggregated by race, ethnicity, sex, disability, and English Learner status. It is a key enforcement tool under civil rights laws prohibiting discrimination based on race, color, national origin, sex, disability, and age.

The Stanford Education Data Archive, produced by the Educational Opportunity Project at Stanford University, is the first national database of academic performance measuring educational opportunity in every community in America across reading and math. ### 409. EdNet — Large-Scale Hierarchical Dataset in Education

```yaml
url: "https://github.com/riiid/ednet"
type: dataset
source: "Riiid"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-02
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-learning-platforms, intelligent-tutoring, k-12, learning-engineering, open-datasets]
```

EdNet is a large-scale dataset of student-system interactions collected over two years by Santa, a multi-platform AI tutoring service with more than 780,000 users in Korea, comprising 131 million interactions from 784,309 students across iOS, Android, and web platforms. The dataset records diverse student actions — including which learning materials were consumed, responses, time spent, and lecture-watching — organized into a four-level hierarchy (KT1 through KT4) of increasing interaction richness. EdNet is described as the largest publicly available education dataset in terms of total students, interactions, and interaction types, and is accompanied by a published paper (arXiv:1912.03072) and an open leaderboard.

### 410. Duolingo Shared Task on Second Language Acquisition Modeling (SLAM)


The 2018 Duolingo Shared Task on Second Language Acquisition Modeling (SLAM) provided participating teams with transcripts from millions of exercises completed by thousands of Duolingo learners over their first 30 days of study, annotated at the token level for mistakes, with the task of predicting future learner errors. Three tracks covered learners of English, Spanish, and French, enabling research into personalized adaptive SLA modeling and language forgetting over time; 15 teams participated and the best systems improved upon a logistic regression baseline by 12%. TALIS is the world's largest international survey about teachers and school leaders. PIAAC is a programme of assessment and analysis of adult skills whose major product is the Survey of Adult Skills — an international computer-based household survey of adults aged 16–65, designed as 10-yearly cycles. The National Teacher and Principal Survey (NTPS) is a system of related questionnaires that provides descriptive data on the context of public and private elementary and secondary education in the United States. The Middle Grades Longitudinal Study of 2017–18 (MGLS:2017) tracked a nationally representative sample of approximately 13,300 sixth-graders across 570 schools to examine the academic, social-emotional, and environmental factors shaping student success and high school readiness during the middle grades transition. ### 428. National Longitudinal Study of the High School Class of 1972 (NLS-72)

```yaml
url: "https://nces.ed.gov/surveys/nls72/"
type: dataset
source: "National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-02
doi: null
license: null
tags: [career-readiness, higher-ed, k-12, longitudinal, open-datasets]
```

The National Longitudinal Study of the High School Class of 1972 (NLS-72) pioneered longitudinal research methodology for examining how high school experiences predict career and educational outcomes, following over 21,000 high school seniors through periodic surveys until 1986, with postsecondary transcripts collected in 1984. The study intentionally oversampled schools serving disadvantaged and minority populations and linked educational experiences with early labor market participation and postsecondary enrollment. Findings include that over 90% of participants engaged in paid work within two years of graduation, and the study established a foundational design replicated in subsequent NCES longitudinal programs.

The NCES locale studies resource hub, "Education Across America: Cities, Suburbs, Towns, and Rural Areas," compiles comparative data for individuals interested in the condition of education across different geographic locales in the United States. ### 436. Current Population Survey (CPS) — Education Supplements

```yaml
url: "https://nces.ed.gov/surveys/cps/"
type: dataset
source: "National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-02
doi: null
license: null
tags: [early-childhood, english-learners, higher-ed, k-12, longitudinal, open-datasets]
```

The Current Population Survey (CPS) is a monthly household survey of approximately 50,000–60,000 dwelling units conducted by the Bureau of the Census for the Bureau of Labor Statistics, with NCES funding educational supplements since the late 1960s to provide annual data on school enrollment and educational attainment. The survey's October Supplement gathers school enrollment data across elementary, secondary, and postsecondary levels, plus preschool participation, with supplementary items covering language proficiency, disabilities, computer use and access, student mobility, and private school tuition. The CPS employs a multistage stratified sampling scheme with households rotating in-sample for four months, out for eight, and back for four more, producing nationally representative estimates of the civilian noninstitutionalized population.

LaNA is an international assessment of emerging mathematics and reading comprehension skills at the end of primary school (grades 4–6 depending on context), designed for countries that need timely, reliable, nationally representative, and internationally comparable education data. A dataset of 13 million student learning traces from Duolingo, capturing vocabulary practice sessions across multiple language pairs. ### 464. Education at a Glance (EAG)

```yaml
url: "https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/serials/education-at-a-glance_g1gha6b0.html"
type: dataset
source: "OECD"
url_confirmed: false
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-03
doi: null
license: null
tags: [early-childhood, higher-ed, k-12, open-datasets]
```

Education at a Glance is OECD's authoritative annual statistical compendium on education systems worldwide, published each September. Each edition provides more than 100 internationally harmonised indicators covering the output of educational institutions; the impact of learning on earnings and employment; access, participation, and progression through education levels; financial resources invested in education; and teachers, learning environments, and school organisation. Data are drawn from the joint UNESCO-OECD-Eurostat (UOE) administrative data collection and from OECD's own surveys (PISA, TALIS, PIAAC), and cover OECD member countries plus a range of partner economies. The 2025 edition (released September 2025, 542 pages) is the most recent. Researchers use EAG as the primary cross-national reference for structural and system-level education indicators.

### 465. PISA for Development (PISA-D)

```yaml
url: "https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/pisa-d-pisa-for-development.html"
type: dataset
source: "OECD"
url_confirmed: false
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-03
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, open-datasets]
```

PISA for Development (PISA-D) is an adapted version of the PISA assessment designed to support low- and middle-income countries in using internationally comparable assessment data to monitor progress toward national targets and SDG 4. PISA-D uses the same proficiency scales as standard PISA but adds more granular performance descriptors at the lower end of the scale, enhanced questionnaire instruments relevant to developing-country contexts, and — uniquely — an out-of-school component assessing 14–16-year-olds who are not enrolled. Nine countries participated in the school-based assessment (Bhutan, Cambodia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Senegal, Zambia); five conducted the out-of-school assessment (Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Senegal). School-based results were released December 2018; out-of-school results in 2020. Public-use files in SAS and SPSS formats are freely downloadable and include student, principal, teacher, parent, and out-of-school respondent records, codebooks, questionnaires, and data compendia.

### 466. TALIS Starting Strong

```yaml
url: "https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/TALIS-Starting-Strong-Database.html"
type: dataset
source: "OECD"
url_confirmed: false
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-03
doi: null
license: null
tags: [early-childhood, open-datasets, professional-development]
```

TALIS Starting Strong is an international large-scale survey of staff and leaders in early childhood education and care (ECEC), conducted under the OECD Teaching and Learning International Survey programme. Its goal is to generate robust internationally comparable data on the ECEC workforce to inform policy on staff working conditions, professional development, pedagogical practices and beliefs, well-being, job satisfaction, and intent to remain in the profession. The survey also addresses diversity in ECEC settings, use of digital technologies, and leadership practices. The 2024 cycle collected data from approximately 17 countries and subnational entities; an earlier 2018 cycle is also available. Public-use files in CSV, Rds, and SPSS formats are downloadable for both cycles, alongside questionnaires, conceptual frameworks, technical reports, and user guides. The dataset is closely related to TALIS (which covers primary and secondary teachers) but focuses exclusively on ECEC settings.

### 467. Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES)

```yaml
url: "https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/oecd-survey-on-social-and-emotional-skills.html"
type: dataset
source: "OECD"
url_confirmed: false
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-03
doi: null
license: null
tags: [formative-assessment, k-12, open-datasets]
```

The OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES) is the largest global initiative to gather comparable cross-national data on the social and emotional skill development of 10- and 15-year-old students. The survey measures a broad set of skills organised into five domains: task performance (persistence, responsibility, self-control, achievement motivation), emotional regulation (stress resistance, emotional control, optimism), engaging with others (assertiveness, sociability, energy), open-mindedness (curiosity, creativity, tolerance), and collaboration. Contextual data are collected from students, teachers, school principals, and (optionally) parents. Round 1 (2019) covered 10 cities/regions; Round 2 (2023) expanded to 16 sites across six countries and ten sub-national entities — including Bulgaria, Chile, Peru, Spain, Mexico, Ukraine, and cities in Colombia, India, UAE, Italy, Japan, Finland, China, Indonesia, and Brazil — surveying approximately 18,000 ten-year-olds and 52,000 fifteen-year-olds. Datasets for both rounds are available on request from OECD. The SSES 2023 database page and 2019 database page provide application and access details.

### 468. OECD Online Education Database (UOE)

```yaml
url: "https://search.oecd.org/education/database.htm"
type: dataset
source: "OECD"
url_confirmed: false
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-03
doi: null
license: null
tags: [higher-ed, k-12, open-datasets]
```

The OECD Online Education Database is the annual administrative data collection underpinning Education at a Glance indicators. Conducted jointly by OECD, the UNESCO Institute for Statistics, and Eurostat (the UOE joint data collection), it has run in its current form since 1993. The collection comprises approximately 25 electronic questionnaires covering student enrolments (nine questionnaires), student entrants (four), graduates (three), personnel (three), education finance (three), class sizes (two), and general population data (one). Data are reported by Ministries of Education or national statistical offices according to international standards and the ISCED classification. Indicators derived from UOE cover educational outputs, access, participation and progression, human and financial resources invested in education, and structural features of national education systems. Raw UOE data are available through the OECD Education data portal and through the OECD.Stat platform; methodological guidance is provided in the UOE Data Collection Manual.

### 470. National Training, Education, and Workforce Survey (NTEWS)

```yaml

tags: [career-readiness, higher-ed, longitudinal, open-datasets]
```

NTEWS is a biennial household survey co-sponsored by NCES and the National Science Foundation's National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES), administered by the U.S. Census Bureau. It collects data on educational enrollment and attainment, nondegree credential types, work experience programs (apprenticeships and internships), employment characteristics, and demographic characteristics, with particular emphasis on the Skilled Technical Workforce — individuals with advanced science and engineering skills but no bachelor's degree. The pilot phase launched in 2022 targeting adults ages 16–75, with the next collection planned for spring 2024; pilot estimates are designated experimental statistics pending quality review.

### 475. District Court Order Desegregation Data

```yaml

description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary

doi: null

tags: [k-12, longitudinal, open-datasets]
```

A dataset cataloging all medium-to-large U.S. school districts ever placed under a court-ordered desegregation plan, covering 358 court cases affecting 850 school districts plus 207 HEW actions since 1978. Each record includes case name, state, NCES district ID, year of initial case, current plan status, and dismissal date; data were compiled from case dockets, Department of Justice records, NAACP Legal Defense materials, and U.S. Department of Education files and verified against Westlaw. ### 480. Who Becomes an Inventor — Innovation Rates by Childhood Location and Demographics

```yaml

type: dataset
```

```yaml
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-03
doi: null
license: null
tags: [higher-ed, k-12, longitudinal, open-datasets]
```

A dataset tracking more than one million U.S. inventors by linking patent records to tax records and school district records, providing innovation rates organized by childhood commuting zone and state, gender, parental income quintile, educational institution attended, and career trajectory including income distributions. The data reveal that children from high-income families are significantly more likely to become inventors, largely due to exposure to innovation rather than innate ability — the so-called "lost Einsteins" phenomenon. ### 506. Analyzing Strategies in MATHia with BERT

```yaml
url: "https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-98465-5_15"
type: paper
source: "AIMS Collaboratory"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-06
doi: null
license: null
tags: [aims, carnegie-learning, math-strategies, nlp]
```

Presents ASTRA (AI-based Strategy Analysis), which uses BERT-based representation learning to discover and analyze math problem-solving strategies at scale in intelligent tutoring system data. The researchers pre-trained BERT using masked language modeling on 6th and 7th-grade student action sequences from Carnegie Learning's MATHia platform, then fine-tuned the embeddings to distinguish successful from unsuccessful strategies. Results showed that single-task strategies predominantly led to success while mixed-task approaches were associated with unsuccessful attempts, with the fine-tuned model achieving approximately 80% accuracy.

### 508. De-identifying Student Personally Identifying Information in Discussion Forum Posts with Large Language Models

```yaml
url: "https://www.emerald.com/ils/article/126/5-6/401/1246753/De-identifying-student-personally-identifying"
type: paper
source: "AIMS Collaboratory"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-06
doi: null
license: null
tags: [aims, llm-application, pii-privacy]
```

Evaluates the effectiveness of three large language models (GPT-4o, Llama 3.3 70B, and Llama 3.1 8B) in redacting personally identifying information from discussion forum posts in massive open online courses. All models achieved high recall rates exceeding 0.9, successfully identifying PII instances overlooked by humans, but precision was considerably lower (0.262 to 0.579) due to over-redaction of non-PII names and locations. The findings suggest LLMs show promise for de-identification tasks, particularly through hybrid human-AI approaches, though context-dependent performance variations indicate careful evaluation is necessary for new applications.

### 528. Linguistic Features Predicting Math Word Problem Readability Among Less-Skilled Readers

```yaml
url: "https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2025/proceedings/2025.EDM.short-papers.189/index.html"
type: paper
source: "AIMS Collaboratory"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-06
doi: null
license: null
tags: [aims, math-word-problems, nlp]
```

Investigates which linguistic features predict math word problem readability for struggling readers, using data from 297,072 students in an intelligent tutoring system. A random forest model achieved the best performance (AUC = .75), revealing that traditional readability metrics were not important to the model's performance. Instead, word count emerged as the most predictive feature, followed by custom semantic magnitude and lexical diversity measures, suggesting that specialized readability assessments for math problems differ substantially from conventional approaches.

### 571. Literacy Express


Literacy Express is a comprehensive preschool curriculum for ages 3–5 that delivers instruction through units covering oral language, emergent literacy, basic math, science, general knowledge, and socioemotional development, accompanied by professional development, teaching materials, and classroom management guidance. Lindamood Phoneme Sequencing (LiPS), formerly called Auditory Discrimination in Depth, teaches students to decode words by identifying individual sounds using the oral-motor aspects of sounds to identify and order them within words, along with instruction in letter patterns, sight words, and context clues, targeting kindergarten through grade 3 and struggling or dyslexic readers. Literacy Design Collaborative (LDC) provides professional development, coaching, and resources to support teachers working collaboratively in their schools to design and implement high-quality, standards-aligned literacy instruction materials focused on reading, research, and writing skills for students in grades 4–8. The WWC reviewed 5 eligible studies, with 3 meeting standards, and found mixed effects on general literacy achievement and no discernible effects on general social studies achievement. The mixed literacy finding across a relatively robust evidence base (3 qualifying studies) suggests LDC may be effective for some implementation contexts but not consistently across all schools.

### 605. Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS)

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/712"

description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, rct, sel, wwc]
```

Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS) is an elementary curriculum for grades 1–5 that delivers short lessons focused on self-control, emotional literacy, social competence, positive peer relations, and interpersonal problem-solving skills to enhance social-emotional competencies and reduce aggression and behavior problems. The WWC reviewed 13 eligible studies, with 2 meeting standards, and found no discernible effects on academic achievement, social interactions, observed individual behavior, or emotional status for elementary students. The null findings across all four outcome domains are notable given the program's widespread adoption in U.S. schools.

Xtreme Reading is a supplemental literacy curriculum for struggling readers in grades 6–12 designed to improve vocabulary, decoding, fluency, and reading comprehension through teacher-led whole-group instruction, cooperative group work, paired practice, and independent practice along with social skills training and motivational components. ### 609. Social Belonging Intervention


Social Belonging interventions aim to reduce the impacts of negative stereotypes that burden students from underrepresented groups — including racial and ethnic minorities, women in engineering, and first-generation college students — and affect their persistence in postsecondary education. The WWC reviewed 11 eligible studies, with 7 meeting standards, and found mixed effects on academic achievement, no discernible effects on college enrollment, and mixed effects on progression in college. ### 613. System of Least Prompts

```yaml
url: "https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/685"
type: report
source: "What Works Clearinghouse"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: llm-summary
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, rct, wwc]
```

System of Least Prompts (SLP), also known as least-to-most prompting, is an instructional practice for students with intellectual disabilities in which teachers establish a structured hierarchy of prompts starting with the least assistive and increasing support until the student performs the skill correctly. The WWC found no qualifying group design studies, and single-case design studies did not reach the threshold required for an evidence rating in any outcome domain. Despite the absence of group-design evidence, SLP is widely used in special education for skill acquisition across academic and functional tasks.


Reciprocal Teaching is an interactive instructional method for improving reading comprehension in which the teacher and students take turns leading a dialogue regarding segments of the text, teaching four core strategies: generating questions, summarizing, clarifying, and predicting, reviewed here for students with specific learning disabilities. ```

Residential Learning Communities (also called living-learning programs) are postsecondary programs that integrate students' academic and residential environments by having students live together in dormitories, take classes together, and participate in structured co-curricular and extracurricular activities designed to strengthen academic engagement and social connection. ### 621. SIPPS (Systematic Instruction in Phonological Awareness, Phonics, and Sight Words)


SIPPS is a structured-literacy reading curriculum using explicit instruction in phonological awareness, phonics, and sight words to support both new and struggling readers across three developmental levels, with flexible grouping based on individual student needs. ### 656. Coherence by Design

```yaml
url: "https://tntp.org/publication/coherence-by-design/"
type: report
source: "TNTP"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: page-abstract
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12]
```

Achievement and opportunity gaps were exacerbated by the pandemic, and students who were already furthest behind have struggled the most to recover. In schools across the country, instructional incoherence, particularly across core classrooms, intervention, and other academic supports, undermines learning acceleration and widens opportunity gaps. Coherence by Design: Building Instructional Systems That Help Students Catch Up makes the case that districts can transform students’ experiences and outcomes by aligning instruction, content, and goals across all learning settings. When systems create the conditions for instructional coherence, every student can engage in grade-level learning. Drawing on national data and real district practice, this publication shows what coherence looks like in classrooms and across systems, why it matters for learning acceleration, and how coherent systems of academic support help educators make better decisions that lead to improved student outcomes. Learn more about how TNTP can help you build coherent instructional systems.

### 657. Teachers’ Time Use

```yaml

description_inferred: false
description_source: page-abstract
date_added: 2026-05-10

license: null
tags: [career-readiness, higher-ed, k-12, sel]
```

Teachers are the backbone of our education system, shaping not only the academic success of millions of students but also their long-term well-being and economic mobility. One out of every 12 college educated workers in the U.S. is a teacher, making educators a vital and influential part of the national workforce. Research shows that teacher quality is the single most important school-based factor in determining students’ motivation, academic achievement, and future outcomes. The impact of great teaching is both immediate and enduring. As TNTP explored in Paths of Opportunity, young people who have access to high-quality academic experiences and excel in school are also more likely to earn a living wage and report high levels of well-being in adulthood. In fact, economists have found that students who move from an average teacher to an excellent teacher in a single grade can expect to earn thousands of additional dollars over their lifetimes.

### 658. Unlocking Algebra

```yaml
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: page-abstract
date_added: 2026-05-10

tags: [higher-ed, k-12, math-education, sel]
```

Mathematics learning is a key part of a strong academic foundation that sets students up to thrive in PK–12 schooling and beyond. As explored in Paths of Opportunity, young people who have access to high-quality academic experiences and excel in school are more likely to earn a living wage and report high levels of well-being in adulthood. Algebra I, specifically, is an inflection point in young people’s education. The course is a gateway to the higher math courses that set students up for college and careers of their choice, including those in the growing STEM sector. ### 666. Accelerate, Don’t Remediate

```yaml
url: "https://tntp.org/publication/accelerate-dont-remediate/"
type: report
source: "TNTP"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: page-abstract
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [k-12, math-education]
```

School systems must decide how to help students catch up from COVID-19. New evidence suggests learning acceleration is the right approach. Research suggests more students have experienced more unfinished learning over the last year than ever before. With the COVID-19 pandemic waning, school systems are facing a critical choice about how to respond. Should they use the traditional approach of reviewing all the content students missed, known as remediation? Or should they start with the current grade’s content and provide “just-in-time” supports when necessary, known as learning acceleration? New data from Zearn, a nonprofit organization whose online math platform is used by one in four elementary students nationwide, provides one of the first direct comparisons of these two approaches—and compelling new evidence that school systems should make learning acceleration the foundation of their academic strategies next year and beyond.

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/01d8e168-631a-467e-81d9-efe3cb195ac4"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10

license: null
tags: [digital-promise, k-12]
```

In this commentary on Interest-Driven Creator (IDC) theory, the authors reflect on the proposed three-step cycles of (i) sparking students’ interest, (ii) fostering individual creativity, and (iii) inculcating lifelong learning habits. Each component of IDC theory pulls together a wide span of prior research and emphasizes active roles for students. Although the context of IDC as a prototype for educational reform is K- 12 Asian classrooms, we note that some US schools are also mired in a focus on test scores. This is especially true among the US most struggling, low-income schools, where a lack of electives and afterschool programs correspond to diminished student perceptions about their own autonomy as learners and their future creative potential. Thus, while IDC is an important provocation for curricular reform in Asia, there is also the need to broaden its scope and begin to explore the potential of IDC as a leadership tool beyond Asia. The wider learning sciences community, the commentary concludes, is uniquely suited to support such an extension, and there are many opportunities for productive international collaboration.

### 711. How Rule Induction Data Mining Can and Cannot Be Useful for Education Research

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/25a027bb-6b5c-42f1-b058-c16843c06e34"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, english-learners]
```

This paper shares insights and recommendations on how rule-induction data mining can and cannot be useful to education research, based on re-analyzing two regression studies with rule induction approaches. Processes and findings were compared to identify whether, in what ways, and why rule-induction could add value. I found that rule-based approaches can provide unique descriptions of the sample that shows at-a-glance, how key predictors relate to each other and to the outcome. They can also identify relationships between variables that held for some subgroups but not others. It was important to clearly understand the difference between mining rules and mining rulesets, as well as the unique research questions that these answer, so that they complement rather than replacement regression.

### 725. An Efficacy Study of a Digital Core Curriculum for Grade 5 Mathematics

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/3496dde6-adb7-4e5d-8be7-fbcbfe97f627"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, formative-assessment, k-12, math-education, rct]
```

The Math Curriculum Impact Study was a large-scale randomized controlled trial (RCT) to test the efficacy of a digital core curriculum for Grade 5 mathematics. Reasoning Mind’s Grade 5 Common Core Curriculum was a comprehensive, adaptive, blended learning approach that schools in the treatment group implemented for an entire school year. Schools in the control group implemented their business-as-usual mathematics curriculum. The study was completed in 46 schools throughout West Virginia, resulting in achievement data from 1,919 students. It also included exploratory investigations of teacher practice and student engagement. The main experimental finding was a null result; achievement was similar in both experimental groups. The exploratory investigations help clarify interpretation of this result. As educational leaders throughout the United States adopt digital mathematics curricula and adaptive, blended approaches, our findings provide a relevant caution. However, our findings are not generalizable to all digital offerings, and there is a continuing need for refined theory, study of implementation, and rigorous experimentation to advise schools.

### 726. CLICKSTREAM: Essential Educational Infrastructure to Promote Student Learning and Educational Theory Development

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/364da4aa-5808-431f-8f13-2d0af99469de"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, higher-ed, k-12, personalized-learning]
```

Theories of learning often frame the student’s journey as a "hero’s quest," yet capturing these idiosyncratic narratives at scale remains a grand challenge for educators. This paper introduces CLICKSTREAM (Cyberinfrastructure for Learning Insights & Curricular Knowledge using Student Trace-data for Research in Educational Analytics & Measurement), a digital learning platform (DLP) designed to transform raw student interaction data into rich, context-aware "stories." Unlike traditional platforms, CLICKSTREAM utilizes a collaborative co-design process where instructors tag digital assets (e.g., videos, quizzes) based on their specific role within a course’s instructional design and timeline. This enrichment allows for: - Instructional Adaptivity: Providing "design-loop" and "step-loop" insights that help instructors adjust teaching strategies in real-time or between semesters. - Predictive Support: Identifying struggling students early through theory-aligned feature engineering. - Theoretical Advancement: Enabling researchers to test complex assumptions of learning theories—such as self-regulated learning—across diverse contexts. By integrating artificial intelligence to automate tagging and fostering interoperability with other DLPs like OpenStax and Terracotta, CLICKSTREAM aims to build a scalable ecosystem where data-driven storytelling empowers educators to provide personalized support for every learner’s unique quest.

### 732. An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects


This report shares the learnings across 28 exploratory projects from teams across K-12 school districts, nonprofits, and nonprofit and for-profit edtech companies, leveraging AI to support numerous goals across K-12 educational settings. Through this report, we aim to highlight the early successes of AI, surface the key barriers that call for cross-disciplinary and collective problem-solving, and consider the potential for each sector to drive forward an equitable future for AI in education. Preliminary findings from these projects show early evidence of AI’s effectiveness in various tasks, including translation, speech recognition, personalization, organizing and summarizing large qualitative datasets, and streamlining tasks to allow teachers more time with their students. ### 741. Rubrics on Historical Thinking Skills for Assignments and Student Work: Initial Validity Evidence

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/45109858-97c6-4f29-b3ce-2e990cf1a579"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, formative-assessment, k-12]
```

Digital Promise sought to create and validate two sets of Historical Thinking Skills rubrics for use in its evaluation of Gates Ventures’ World History Project (WHP) curriculum: one for evaluating teacher-assigned activities, and another for evaluating the student work those activities produced. Adopting a principled assessment development approach called Evidence Centered Design (Mislevy et al., 2003), the Digital Promise team began by conducting an academic literature review to inform rubric design, then piloted the draft rubrics to test their validity by having expert world history teachers score a sample of world history assignments and associated student work and provide feedback on the rubrics and scoring process. We found that scores that trained raters assigned to activities and student work were generally consistent across scorers, and scorer feedback indicated that the rubrics did indeed measure valuable historical thinking skills. Based on an analysis of rubric scores and scorer feedback, our team revised the draft rubrics to their final form.

### 743. AI and the Future of Learning: Expert Panel Report

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/4b4d5758-dc24-400c-92bb-206edba192aa"

source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true

date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null

```

This report is based on the discussion that emerged from a convening of a panel of 22 experts in artificial intelligence (AI) and in learning. It introduces three layers that can frame the meaning of AI for educators. First, AI can be seen as “computational intelligence” and capability can be brought to bear on educational challenges as an additional resource to an educator’s abilities and strengths. Second, AI brings specific, exciting new capabilities to computing, including sensing, recognizing patterns, representing knowledge, making and acting on plans, and supporting naturalistic interactions with people. Third, AI can be used as a toolkit to enable us to imagine, study, and discuss futures for learning that don’t exist today. Experts voiced the opinion that the most impactful uses of AI in education have not yet been invented. The report enumerates important strengths and weaknesses of AI, as well as the respective opportunities and barriers to applying AI to learning. Through discussions among experts about these layers, we observed new design concepts for using AI in learning. The panel also made seven recommendations for future research priorities.

### 746. Teaching Partner, Grading Assistant, Substitute Teacher: Three Ways Teachers Positioned an Artificial Intelligence Tool in Writing Instruction

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/4f2d86a3-9b66-4538-a5ad-977bb8fbacf7"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, formative-assessment, k-12, literacy]
```

This study investigates how teachers understand and position AI tools in middle school writing instruction, drawing on 27 teacher interviews collected during a study called Project Topeka that used an interactive argumentative writing platform with AI-generated scores and feedback. Based on the interviews, we generate an initial theoretical framework of how teachers position AI tools — and therefore themselves — in their teaching. We found that some teachers leveraged AI as a “teaching partner” that provided insights to help enhance teaching and learning while remaining central to instruction themselves and interacting with students in numerous ways. Others delegated aspects of assessment and learning to AI as a “grading assistant” to save time and increase efficiency, interacting with students with a slight emphasis on score attainment over skill development. Another group turned instruction over to the AI tool as if it were a “substitute teacher,” interacting minimally with students and placing themselves on the instructional periphery. We describe each approach in detail and discuss implications for teaching practices, teachers’ roles, the profession, and students’ experiences and opportunities.

### 748. Navigating the Tensions: How Could Equity-relevant Research Also Be Agile, Open, and Scalable?

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/5173898e-346f-45e0-8aa5-f5eead7e0016"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, higher-ed, k-12]
```

Digital learning platforms are beginning to become open to research. Specifically, in our work in SEERNet, developers are extending five platforms, each used in either K-12 or higher education by more than 100,000 users, to enable third-party researchers to explore, develop, and test improvements. SEERNet seeks to enable equity-relevant research aligned with the IES Standards for Excellence in Education Research (SEER) principles. It also seeks to support research that is more agile (or rapid), is more open, and scales from research to impacts on practice. We review the emerging tensions among the goal of equity-relevant research and desires for agile, open, and scalable research. We argue that designing and developing technical capabilities for agile, open, and scalable research will not be enough. Based on a series of interviews we conducted with experts in social sciences and equity-focused research, we argue that researchers will have to rethink how they plan and undertake their research. Five shifts could help. First, researchers could deliberately reframe their designs away from a comprehensive, monolithic study to smaller, agile cycles that test a smaller conjecture each time. Second, researchers could shift from designing new educational resources to determining how well-used resources could be elaborated and refined to address equity issues. Third, researchers could utilize variables that capture student experiences to investigate equity when they cannot obtain student demographic variables. Fourth, researchers could work in partnership with educators on equity problems that educators prioritize and want help in solving. Fifth, researchers could acknowledge that achieving equity is not only a technological or resource-design problem, but requires working at the classroom and systems levels too. In SEERNet, we look forward to working with the research community to find ways to address equity through research using well-used digital learning platforms, and to simultaneously conduct research that is more agile, more open, and more directly applicable at scale.

### 758. Instructional Coherence and Shared Responsibilities: OBC's Impact on EdTech Procurement

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/5ab830f6-3f5d-4286-880b-bbf6b9105a19"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, k-12]
```

This report explores the learnings from the first cohort to leverage outcomes based contracting (OBC) for edtech, where payment terms are partially predicated on meeting specific student achievement benchmarks. The research found that the OBC model served as a powerful lever for instructional coherence, driving edtech implementation rates to levels 10 times higher than the national average. By fostering mutual accountability and breaking down silos within districts and across districts and providers, the model enables district, school, and provider teams to move beyond a simple buyer-seller relationship toward a data-driven partnership focused on student outcomes. While districts experienced challenges selecting student populations and outcomes and ensuring implementation met dosage requirements, the findings demonstrate that the OBC model empowers district leaders to make more intentional resource allocation decisions. Ultimately, this innovative approach ensures that edtech investments are no longer measured by licenses purchased, but by their measured impact on student learning outcomes.

This literature review examines the effectiveness, affordances, and challenges of experiential learning environments and simulations in K-12 education, situating Operation Outbreak within the broader learning sciences tradition. Simulation-based learning has been shown as a way to connect theory with practice by immersing students in environments where they can apply knowledge, collaborate, and make decisions with real consequences. ### 761. Principal Leadership in a Virtual Environment

The sudden and unexpected shift to remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic has brought new awareness of the need for school leaders who can ensure that high-quality, equitable education can take place virtually as well as in the classroom. How can school districts develop a large corps of such principals? Research on the topic is still emerging, and this report offers early considerations for decision-makers based on an examination of research literature, interviews with 11 principals and administrators knowledgeable about virtual learning, and Digital Promise’s experiences in the field. ### 764. Strategic Surprise and the Future of Educational R&D

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/5f4a2b76-ee88-4c0c-8cfa-6712401fdb61"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, k-12]
```

For decades, education R&D has delivered mostly incremental change, consistent with Tyack and Cuban’s observation in Tinkering Towards Utopia (1995) that systems tend to assimilate new technologies. Some innovation initiatives aim to engineer “planned serendipity”—structuring teams and infrastructure so that unexpected insights are more likely to arise and propagate (Michael H. Levine, personal communication, 2025). Today’s environment is different: generative AI, platform‑level data, and new research infrastructures are creating strategic surprises–rapid shifts that outpace traditional sensing and response. We propose re‑architecting education R&D for agility, responsiveness, and breakthrough potential. Drawing on ARPA‑style (federal Advanced Research Projects Agencies) (NASEM, 2017) models (and our work with SEERNet and Advanced Education Research and Development Fund (AERDF), we contrast legacy approaches with a surprise‑ready architecture along four dimensions: (1) framing commitments, (2) problem definition, (3) project/talent model, and (4) focal outcomes. We illustrate with six “ripe problem” examples that compress the observe–orient–decide–act loop in schools, and we conclude with role‑specific recommendations for researchers, developers, funders, and systems leaders. Our goal is a field that not only studies change, but orchestrates the conditions—capable people and enabling environments—under which transformative learning improvements can emerge.

### 767. Unveiling the Value of Exploration: Insights from NSF-Funded Research on Emerging Technologies for Teaching and Learning

This report investigates how interdisciplinary, exploratory projects contribute to the National Science Foundation’s (NSF) mission of building scientific knowledge and translating research into practice. The Center for Integrative Research in Computing and Learning Sciences (CIRCLS) examined the overall portfolio and interviewed PIs funded by NSF across five key topics: Artificial Intelligence, Virtual and Augmented Reality, Collaborative Learning, Accessibility and Learning, and Simulations. Bringing inquiry learning environments to scale is an important issue for society, especially given the needs for stronger inquiry skills among future citizens, employees, and leaders. This chapter argues that scaling is particularly challenging for ambitious inquiry learning innovations that often do not find a good fit with prevailing priorities in many of today’s classrooms and communities. ### 780. Language and Mathematics Learning: A Comparative Study of Digital Learning Platforms


This paper presents a conceptual exploration of how Digital Learning Platforms (DLPs) can be utilized to investigate the impact of language clarity, precision, engagement, and contextual relevance on mathematics learning from word problems. Focusing on three distinct DLPs—ASSISTments/E-TRIALS, MATHia/UpGrade, and Canvas/Terracotta—we propose hypothetical studies aimed at uncovering how nuanced language modifications can enhance mathematical understanding and engagement. ### 786. Generalizability of a Technology-Based Intervention to Enhance Conceptual Understanding in Mathematics

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/7a123d3c-22ec-46db-b7cf-709c3aa65583"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, k-12, math-education]
```

Three previously reported experiments found that a technology-enhanced intervention increased student conceptual understanding of mathematics in Texas. To investigate generalizability to broader populations and settings, we triangulate among three methods. First, we examine interactions between demographic variables and intervention effects. We found that the intervention was not sensitive to typical variations in school populations. Second, we use propensity score methods to measure the match between the sample and a broader population. The sample matches the school population in Texas, with minor exceptions; we report adjusted effect sizes. Third, quasi-experimental research with populations outside of Texas are considered. Results from Florida and England were consistent with Texas findings. Across three methods, the results suggest that the experimental findings generalize across populations and settings. This work also establishes a practical approach to investigating generalizability in experimental research in schools.

### 801. Evaluation of an Online Tutoring Program in Elementary Mathematics

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/83873e9c-c786-4edd-92df-d8dd68854483"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, formative-assessment, k-12, math-education, meta-analysis, rct]
```

Many students struggle with mathematics in late elementary school, particularly on the topic of fractions. In a best evidence syntheses of research on increasing achievement in elementary school mathematics, Pelligrini et al. (2018) highlighted tutoring as a way to help students. Online tutoring is attractive because costs may be lower and logistics easier than with face-to-face tutoring. Cignition developed an approach that combines online 1:1 tutoring with a fractions game, called FogStone Isle. The game provides students with additional learning opportunities and provides tutors with information that they can use to plan tutoring sessions. A randomized controlled trial investigated the research question: Do students who participate in online tutoring and a related mathematical game learn more about fractions than students who only have access to the game? Participants were 144 students from four schools, all serving low-income students with low prior mathematics achievement. In the Treatment condition, students received 20-25 minute tutoring sessions twice per week for an average of 18 sessions and also played the FogStone Isle game. In the Control condition, students had access to the game, but did not play it often. Control students did not receive tutoring. Students were randomly assigned to condition after being matched on pre-test scores. The same diagnostic assessment was used as a pre-test and as a post-test. The planned analysis looked for differences in gain scores (post-test minus pre-test scores) between conditions. We conducted a t-test on the aggregate gain scores, comparing conditions; the results were statistically significant (t = 4.0545, df = 132.66, p-value <.001). To determine an effect size, we treated each site as a study in a meta-analysis. Using gain scores, the effect size was g=+.66. A more sophisticated treatment of the pooled standard deviation resulted in a corrected effect size of g=.46 with a 95% confidence interval of [+.23,+.70]. Students who received online tutoring and played the related Fog Stone Isle game learned more; our research found the approach to be efficacious. The Pelligrini et al. (2018) meta-analysis of elementary math tutoring programs found g =.26 and was based largely on face-to-face tutoring studies. Thus, this study compares favorably to prior research on face-to-face mathematics tutoring with elementary students. Limitations are discussed; in particular, this is an initial study of an intervention under development. Effects could increase or decrease as development continues and the program scales. Although this study was planned long before the current pandemic, results are particularly timely now that many students are at home under shelter-in-place orders due to COVID-19. The approach taken here is feasible for students at home, with tutors supporting them from a distance. It is also feasible in many other situations where equity could be addressed directly by supporting students via online tutors.

---

---

### 813. Delivering virtual K-8 computing professional development in rural KY

```yaml
url: "https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/90b614f8-9549-4924-a07f-400275d000db"
type: report
source: "Digital Promise"
url_confirmed: true
description_inferred: false
description_source: listing
date_added: 2026-05-10
doi: null
license: null
tags: [digital-promise, formative-assessment, k-12, professional-development]
```

Teachers living and working in rural areas in the United States often lack access to high-quality professional development (PD) opportunities. As computer science (CS) and computational thinking (CT) education pathways increasingly develop in rural districts, it is essential to provide quality PD for their teachers so they can identify opportunities for and plan to embed CS and CT learning in their classrooms. A key element in delivering high-quality PD is understanding the specific educational and wider cultural needs of the community where it will be delivered, something we call “mining cultural capital”. In this poster, we report on the delivery of four 30-minute virtual PD sessions within two rural school districts in Eastern Kentucky: Pikeville Independent and Floyd County Schools. The virtual sessions were specifically geared toward elementary and middle school teachers. The sessions were led by a long-time educator in the region who worked to curate relevant examples and delivered the PD via a recorded video conference. The recordings are available for teachers in the region to watch and re-watch as they develop their lessons. Survey results showed that participating teachers found the PD to be valuable. Furthermore, feedback from teachers suggests that access to these short just-in-time PD sessions provided valuable learning opportunities and also sparked new lesson ideas for teachers.
